1128.title: The Ragmala
1128.hook: the Granth's last page is a garland of raga names, and Sikhs hold more than one view of it
1128.howItsDone: At the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, some congregations recite the Ragmala and others conclude with the Mundavani, following the custom of the place, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada allows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Jaijavanti, and your line was before it slips by. Today, the Granth's very last page.

Two families sit down to the same holiday meal. One says the blessing one way, the other another way, both the way they always have. Nobody leaves the table. The food is shared. The difference is just there, spoken plainly, held kindly. Sikhs have a page like that: the very last page of the Guru Granth Sahib as it is printed, called the Ragmala. Sikhs don't all read it the same way.
screen: `TWO WAYS AT ONE TABLE.` → `THE LAST PAGE OF THE GRANTH.` → `HOW A DIFFERENCE IS HELD.`

segments.voice: After the last raga, Jaijavanti, come collections of verses, then Guru Arjan's Mundavani, which tradition calls the seal on the book, where he says the dish holds truth, contentment and reflection. Then, in the printed Granth, one more page: the Ragmala. The name is usually read as a garland of ragas, and that's what it looks like: a list in verse naming ragas and arranging them in families, with the ragas set alongside related melodies. Here is the difference. Some Sikhs hold that the Ragmala belongs to the Granth as it was handed on, and recite it at the close of a complete reading. Other Sikhs hold that it was added later, that it isn't Gurbani, the Gurus' word, and they close the reading at the Mundavani instead. Both are Sikhs, devoted to the same Guru Granth Sahib. Now the Panth's own answer. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Panth's code of conduct, doesn't silence either side. In paraphrase, it says a full reading may be concluded with the Mundavani or with the Ragmala, according to the custom of the place, and it notes that the Panth holds differing views. It also says no copy of the Granth should be written or printed without the Ragmala. So the code keeps the page in every copy, the question stays open, and the community goes on sitting at one table. Not every difference has to be settled to be lived with.
screen: `MUNDAVANI: THE SEAL ON THE BOOK.` · `A GARLAND OF RAGA NAMES.` · `SOME RECITE IT; SOME CLOSE BEFORE IT.` · `THE PAGE STAYS IN EVERY COPY.` · then, large: `DIFFER WITH RESPECT.`

segments.voice: If you can, open the last page of the Granth online and let your eyes move slowly over the names of the ragas, reading it the way you'd read a family tree in someone else's home: with interest and with care. Then bring to mind one person you disagree with about something that matters, and hold the difference and the person side by side, without letting go of either. If you pray, ask in your own way for a kind heart toward them; if you don't, simply notice that both can be held at once.
Ragmala. The garland of ragas on the Granth's last printed page; some Sikhs recite it, some close the reading before it, and the Rehat Maryada leaves the closing to each place's custom. Today's word.
Your line: differ with respect. The page stays in every copy, and everyone stays at the table. See you tomorrow.

1129.title: Raga kirtan today
1129.hook: the raga name at the top of each hymn is like a recipe card, and teachers and ragis still cook from it, alongside simpler tunes
1129.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis lead kirtan with harmonium and tabla, and some also use stringed instruments and sing each shabad in the raga named in its heading; congregations also sing shabads to simpler tunes everyone can join.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ragmala, and your line was differ with respect. Today, the singers.

A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. The measurements are vague: a handful, enough, until it smells right. The card alone can't make the dish; somebody has to have stood next to her at the stove. And yet as long as someone keeps cooking from it, the card stays alive. For weeks, every hymn on this path has come with a raga name at the top, like the title on that card. Today: who is still cooking from it.
screen: `A RECIPE CARD, SOFT AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE CARD ALONE CAN'T MAKE THE DISH.` → `WHO STILL COOKS FROM IT?`

segments.voice: The Granth gathers its hymns under raga headings: Sri Rag, Majh, Gauri, and on through Kalyan, Prabhati and Jaijavanti. The heading tells the singer the musical mode. The text doesn't write out a melody note by note; like the grandmother's card, it names the dish and trusts that someone knows how to cook it. That knowing lives in people. In the gurdwara, the singers of kirtan are called ragis, and their craft passes from teacher to student. Some ragis and teachers give their lives to singing each shabad in the raga its heading names, often with stringed instruments as well as harmonium and tabla. This way of singing is often called Gurmat Sangeet, the music of the Guru's way, and there are schools and teachers devoted to keeping it. In other gurdwaras and homes, shabads are sung to simpler tunes a whole congregation can pick up. Sikhs hold different views about how closely kirtan should follow the named raga, and the singing goes on both ways, sometimes in the same building on the same day. What both share is the text. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, in paraphrase, says that in the congregation kirtan is the singing of Gurbani, with only certain other writings allowed beside it. The words don't change; the tune is the part handed down by ear. So the raga names on this road aren't museum labels. Somewhere a student may be learning Prabhati for a morning program, and a ragi tuning up for Kalyan at dusk.
screen: `THE HEADING NAMES THE RAGA.` · `RAGIS: TEACHER TO STUDENT.` · `RAGA KIRTAN AND SIMPLER TUNES.` · `THE WORDS STAY; THE TUNE IS HANDED DOWN.` · then, large: `THE OLD TUNES LIVE.`

segments.voice: If you can, search for one shabad sung in the raga its heading names, adding raag kirtan or Gurmat Sangeet to the search, and as it plays, sit still and notice how the voice and the instruments move together, letting the breath follow the music's pace. If you can't play anything, recall a melody you learned from a person rather than a screen. If you pray, listen as kirtan is meant to be heard, as Gurbani sung; if you don't, simply listen like someone being taught.
Raga kirtan today. Shabads sung in the raga named at the top of the hymn, kept alive by ragis, teachers and schools, alongside simpler congregational tunes. Today's word.
Your line: the old tunes live. As long as someone keeps singing, the card stays alive. Same time tomorrow.

1130.title: Your raga
1130.hook: after a whole block of moods, some listeners find one raga that feels like home, and a line in Sri Rag's var says what makes a raga worth it
1130.howItsDone: Listeners of kirtan often come to love particular ragas and particular ragis; in the gurdwara, the raga sung usually follows the hymn's heading and the time of day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, raga kirtan today, and your line was the old tunes live.

Some people come alive before sunrise, with the kettle and the dark window. Others are only themselves after dinner, with the lamps on. Some love a heavy morning with work in it; some wait all year for spring. It just turned out to be home. After weeks walking through the ragas of the Guru Granth Sahib, one mood after another, some listeners find that one of them has quietly become theirs.
screen: `WHICH HOUR IS YOURS?` → `ONE MOOD AFTER ANOTHER.` → `ONE THAT FEELS LIKE HOME.`

segments.voice: Lay out a few of the rooms on this road. Kedara at dusk, tender as the light goes. Bhairao, the serious morning, opening with nothing happens outside you. Basant, where spring is always present. Kalyan in the evening, with a bee that comes back again and again. Prabhati at daybreak, with the Name as an ornament. Jaijavanti, where the ragas end: remember, this is your work. Each one put a mood around the same Word. Now a line from the Granth itself about ragas. In the var of Sri Rag, Guru Amar Das writes, in paraphrase: among the ragas, Sri Rag stands high, if through it one comes to love the True One. Hear the condition. If. The raga's worth isn't in the notes alone; it's in what the singing does to the heart. A raga that leaves you cold hasn't done its work for you yet. A raga that turns you toward the One has. That makes my raga a modest claim. It doesn't say this raga beats the others. It says: this is where, for now, the love arrives most easily for me. Tradition gives ragas their hours and seasons, and the hymns inside them say what they say. But the listener is part of the music too. Your hour of the day, your season, the mood you live in most, may lead you to one raga first. And the Granth's line suggests the test: not which one sounds best, but which one leaves you nearer.
screen: `DUSK, MORNING, SPRING, EVENING, DAWN.` · `SRI RAG STANDS HIGH, IF.` · `THE WORTH IS IN THE LOVE.` · `NOT THE BEST: THE NEAREST.` · then, large: `MY RAGA.`

segments.voice: Let the ragas on this road pass slowly through your mind, the dusk one, the serious morning, spring, evening, dawn, the last raga, and notice which one your breath settles into; if none does, let the hour of the day that feels most like home be your guide. When one rises, say its name once, silently. If you pray, hold it as Guru Amar Das's line suggests, as a way toward love of the True One; if you don't, let the name be a small marker of where you feel at home.
Your raga. The one mood of the Granth's music where, for now, you come nearest; Guru Amar Das says a raga is worth it if through it one comes to love the True One. Today's word.

1131.title: The ragas close
1131.hook: the walk through the Granth's ragas ends: dusk, dawn, spring, rain and a serious morning, all carrying one Word
1131.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the Granth's ragas in kirtan through the day and the year, with different ragas for different hours and seasons, all of them carrying Gurbani, the Guru's Word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your raga, and your line was my raga: the one that leaves you nearer.

Watch one river from the same bridge all day. Gray and quick at dawn. Brown and slow at noon. Gold at evening, then black, with lights on it. Someone passing at each hour could think it was a different river. It's one water, wearing the hours. Since the day this path asked why the Granth is sung, it has walked raga by raga through the pages. Today the ragas close, and the question is what ran through all of them.
screen: `ONE RIVER, CHANGING ALL DAY.` → `ONE WATER, WEARING THE HOURS.` → `WHAT RAN THROUGH ALL OF THEM?`

segments.voice: Look back at the road. It began with why the Granth is sung at all, then the small markings, ghar and rahao, then strings and drums, then the order of the ragas. Then Sri Rag, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on through the book: Sorath and Bilaval, Ramkali and Maru, Tukhari's months, Kedara's dusk, Bhairao's serious morning, Basant's spring, Malar's rain, Kanara, Kalyan's evening, Prabhati's dawn, and Jaijavanti, where the ragas end. Then the Ragmala, held with respect in two ways, the ragis who keep the old tunes alive, and the raga that feels like yours. Each section opens under its own heading, with an invocation of the One, and every one holds hymns that point the same way: toward the Name, the Word, the Shabad. The moods changed. The Word didn't. Guru Nanak has a line in the Japji that fits. In paraphrase: with a single word, the Creator spread out the expanse of creation, and from it rivers beyond counting flowed. One word; many rivers. The Gurus didn't write a different faith for the morning and another for the evening. They set the one Word in mood after mood, so it could meet a person wherever they were: tender at dusk, hopeful in spring, heavy-hearted on a hard morning, quiet before dawn. So when you hear kirtan from now on, the raga name at the top isn't a puzzle to solve. It's the hour the Word has dressed for. Tomorrow a new stretch begins: Guru Nanak's conversation on a mountain, recorded in Ramkali.
screen: `FROM WHY IT'S SUNG TO JAIJAVANTI.` · `EVERY SECTION POINTS TO THE NAME.` · `ONE WORD, MANY RIVERS.` · `THE HOUR THE WORD HAS DRESSED FOR.` · then, large: `MANY MOODS, ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad in a raga you skipped or barely lingered on, and let it be unfamiliar, noticing the mood it brings, without naming it too fast. Then, under the mood, listen for the steady thing: the breath going in and out, the same as in every other raga. If you pray, let the Word, Waheguru, be the river under the changing light; if you don't, let the breath be that river, one water through every hour.
The ragas close. The end of the walk through the Granth's ragas, where every section, in every mood, points to one Word. Today's word.
Your line: many moods, one word. The river changes color all day and stays one water. One stretch done, and the hill goes on.

1132.title: A conversation on the mountain
1132.hook: a circle of yogis sits down, and Guru Nanak's long dialogue with them begins
1132.howItsDone: The Sidh Gosht is sung in kirtan and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs study it in katha, where a teacher explains the yogis' questions and Guru Nanak's answers one stanza at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday the ragas closed, and your line was many moods, one word. Today, a new stretch inside Raga Ramkali.

The circle is already seated when the poem begins. A gathering of Siddhs, yogis who have given up house and family, settle into their postures and greet the company of holy people around them. Then a guest speaks, and his first words aren't to them at all. Guru Nanak bows to the One and says he would cut off his own head and set it down before that One, offering body and mind. Only after that bow does the talking start, and it goes on: question, answer, stanza after stanza.
screen: `THE SIDDHS SIT DOWN.` → `NANAK BOWS TO THE ONE.` → `THEN THE TALKING STARTS.`

segments.voice: The poem is called the Sidh Gosht. Sidh is the yogi, the one said to have reached the goal; gosht is a discussion, a talk. So: the talk with the Siddhs. It sits in the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Ramkali, under Guru Nanak's name. These yogis have come up on this path before, once in a single picture of a lotus and a duck, once in Bhai Gurdas's telling of their meeting on a mountain, and tradition places the conversation up in those heights. First, this is scripture that keeps the other side's questions. The yogis aren't straw men set up to fall over. They ask real, sharp things, the kind a serious seeker would ask: who are you, why do you live like that, where did it all begin. The Granth sets their questions down in their own voice, some of them by name. Second, the manners. The yogis greet the gathering. Nanak bows before he argues. In the second stanza, in paraphrase, he asks what use there is in wandering about, since it's truth that makes a person pure, and without the Word no one is set free. That's a firm view, said plainly, but said sitting down, in a circle, with people who disagree. Third, the shape teaches. Sikh teaching often comes as song to be sung together. Here it comes as dialogue, two sides taking turns, so listening is built into the form: a question has to be heard all the way through before it can be answered.

1133.title: Who are you
1133.hook: the yogis ask Nanak his name, his path, where he comes from and where he goes
1133.howItsDone: In katha on the Sidh Gosht, teachers often linger on this exchange, and Sikhs hear in Guru Nanak's answer the idea of living under hukam, the divine order, rather than defining oneself by caste or lineage.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Sidh Gosht opened, and your line was a conversation. Today the yogis ask their first question.

Name. Place of residence. Purpose of visit. Final destination. A passport desk wants four answers, and it wants them short. The yogis in the Sidh Gosht ask a stranger almost the same list. Who are you? What's your name? What path are you on, and what are you after? Where do you sit, where do you stay, where did you come from, and where are you going? They ask him, in paraphrase, to answer truthfully. Fair questions, for a guest.
screen: `NAME. PATH. PURPOSE.` → `WHERE FROM? WHERE TO?` → `THE YOGIS ASK THE GUEST.`

segments.voice: Listen to what Nanak leaves out. No village, no family name, no caste, no sect, no teacher's lineage. His answer, in paraphrase: the One lives deep in every heart, and that is where I sit and where I stay. I walk in the will of the True Guru. I came in the ease of the divine order, and I go wherever that order sends me. Nanak lives forever under that will. My seat is the One who does not move; that's what the Guru's teaching gave me. And the one who turns toward the Guru comes to understand, recognizes their own self, and merges into the True. They asked where he sits, and he names a seat inside every heart. They asked where he comes from and where he's going, and instead of a road he gives a direction: the hukam, the order that sends him. They asked his path, and he says, more or less, I walk where I'm told. That isn't dodging. It's answering one level down. A name tells you what to call someone; a hometown, where they started. Nanak's answer tells you what he's oriented toward, the one thing a name never says. And near the end, a quiet phrase: aap pachhaanai, a person recognizes their own self. In this poem, knowing who you are isn't something you hand over at the desk. It's reached, by turning toward the Guru. The yogis' question was the right one. It's just bigger than they thought.
screen: `NO VILLAGE, NO CASTE, NO LINEAGE.` · `MY SEAT IS IN EVERY HEART.` · `I GO WHERE THE ORDER SENDS ME.` · `KNOWING YOURSELF IS REACHED.` · then, large: `WHO ARE YOU.`

segments.voice: Let the usual answers to who you are come up and pass by, your name, your job, your town, your role at home; they're all true, so set them down gently for a moment. Then ask again underneath them, the way Nanak answered, by what you're turned toward, and when a line comes, even a clumsy one, hold it for a few breaths. If you pray, set your line down under the hukam, the order Nanak said he walks in.
Who are you. The yogis' first question to Nanak, answered not with a name or a town but with a seat in every heart and a life lived under the divine order. Today's word.
Your line: who are you. The answer isn't on a passport. Rest well.

1134.title: Living in the world
1134.hook: asked how to get through the world, Nanak points to a lotus and a duck in the water
1134.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of this stanza when describing the householder's life, grihasti: working, raising a family and serving others while keeping the Name in mind, rather than withdrawing from the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked who Nanak was, and your line was who are you. Today, the next question.

A duck spends its whole day in the pond. It dives for food, paddles against the current. Then it climbs onto the bank, gives one shake, and the water simply isn't there anymore; the feathers underneath are dry. That small animal answers a serious question in the Sidh Gosht. A yogi named Charpat puts it to Nanak: the world is an ocean, hard to cross, they say, so how does anyone get to the other side?
screen: `IN THE POND ALL DAY.` → `ONE SHAKE, AND DRY.` → `CHARPAT: HOW DO WE CROSS?`

segments.voice: Nanak's reply, in paraphrase: as the lotus stays apart in the water, and as the duck swims in the stream and stays dry, so a person can live. Earlier on this path the lotus had its day, the flower that rises clean out of the mud. Today, look at the duck, because it does something the lotus doesn't. A lotus is rooted; it stays put and lets the water move around it. A duck goes places. It hunts, feeds its young, fights the current. Of the two pictures, the duck is the one with a job. That matters, because the yogis in this poem had answered the world by leaving the household behind, going where the water can't reach. Nanak doesn't tell them they're wrong to love stillness. He points at a bird completely in the water that comes out dry. You don't have to leave the stream to stay untouched by it. The same stanza adds a phrase: living with hopes all around and not being ruled by them, keeping the One settled in the mind. That's the duck's secret said without the bird. The hopes, worries and deadlines are real water; they just don't get under the feathers. And look where the week has been heading: the last of the ragas, many moods and one Word; a circle on the mountain; the question who are you. Today's answer gives that self somewhere to live: not a cave, not a peak, but the stream. In Sikh teaching that picture belongs to the householder, the person with work, a family and bills, who keeps the Name in mind through all of it.
screen: `THE LOTUS STAYS. THE DUCK SWIMS.` · `NO NEED TO LEAVE THE STREAM.` · `HOPES ALL AROUND, NOT RULED BY THEM.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PICTURE.` · then, large: `THE DUCK STAYS DRY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the busiest stretch waiting for you, the commute, the inbox, the kitchen at dinnertime, and picture yourself right in it, moving and working, then picture the duck paddling hard and the water rolling off its back. Breathe in: in the stream; breathe out: dry underneath, for a few slow rounds. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath.

Your line: the duck stays dry. In the stream all day, and dry underneath. Until tomorrow.
